what_source_actually_states: The Letter reports heat-pulse propagation in a purer NaF crystal than the one used by McNelly et al. Its abstract (p. 26) states that propagation of heat pulses in NaF has been studied to higher temperatures in a purer crystal and that at the highest temperatures the second-sound velocity fails to level off at the theoretically predicted limiting value. On p. 26 the traces are identified by temperature: 9.6 K shows the longitudinal and transverse first-sound pulses, the transverse pulse broadens by 12.5 K, and at 15 K a new pulse 'which we identify as second sound' appears. On p. 27 the authors state that at 18 K the arrival time for the peak of the second-sound pulse is essentially at the value expected from existing theory but has yet to level off. So the paper does report second sound in NaF, which is the whole of what the manuscript sentence claims.

notes: register row CR095. 3 pages read in full (26-28). No numeric second-sound velocity is printed in the text; the velocity information is carried by Fig. 3 (p. 27, arrival time vs temperature, 8-20 K), which was not digitised. The DOI is printed only on the publisher record, not on the page.

manuscript_statement: Second sound was observed in sodium fluoride (McNelly et al. 1970) and a further observation in graphite above 100 K (Huberman et al. 2019) extends the window to a much higher temperature.

source_wording_max25words: We directly observed second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K using time-resolved optical measurements
what_source_actually_states: The title is 'Observation of second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K' and the abstract (p. 1) states that the authors directly observed second sound in graphite above 100 K using time-resolved optical measurements of thermal transport on the micrometre scale, with results in qualitative agreement with ab initio calculations. The body text (p. 3) reports damped oscillations of the transient thermal grating at 85 K, gives a velocity of about 3200 m/s from the slope of the frequency-wave-vector fit, and states that the calculated second-sound velocity from the ab initio resonance is 3650 m/s, 'somewhat higher than the measured velocity'. On p. 4 the oscillatory behaviour is reported as still apparent at 104 K and 125 K and gone at 150 K. This is exactly the claim: an observation above 100 K that extends the window well beyond the 11-14.5 K NaF range.
